passage:
Astrid told herself it was love. She checked Vera's phone only because people online could be dangerous. She kept Vera's bank card in the kitchen drawer because Vera was bad with money. She had steered her towards the grey coat instead of the red one, because red drew looks. And Vera's friends from the choir? Astrid simply mentioned how tired Vera always seemed after seeing them.
Tonight Vera asked, carefully, "Can I go to Mette's birthday on Friday?"
Can I. Astrid noticed the words. A year ago Vera sang solos, argued about books, cycled home at midnight.
"If you want," Astrid said, and watched Vera's shoulders stay tight, as if even a yes was a test.
Later, alone in the kitchen of the Oslo flat, Astrid opened the drawer and looked at the card. Under the word love she could hear something colder: if Vera needs me for everything, she can't leave.

qa.q: Where did Astrid keep Vera's bank card?
qa.a: She kept Vera's bank card in the kitchen drawer.

qa.q: What does Astrid feel underneath her idea of love?
qa.a: Astrid fears losing Vera; the colder thought is that if Vera needs her for everything, Vera can't leave.

qa.q: What turning point could Astrid act on after looking at the card?
qa.a: Astrid could hand back the card and stop checking the phone, and seek help from a counsellor for the fear of losing Vera, instead of tightening control.

qa.q: How has Vera's life changed over the year?
qa.a: Vera once sang solos and cycled home at midnight; now she asks permission to go to a birthday and stays tense even at a yes.

grounding: A woman controls Vera's phone, money, clothes and friends while calling it love, and glimpses the fear of losing power underneath.

passage:
The family counselling centre had a fish tank, and Ira watched the fish instead of Tenzin.
The counsellor had asked Tenzin to describe an ordinary day. Tenzin spoke slowly. "I send Ira a photo when I reach work. I share my location. Ira checks my expenses every Sunday. I don't wear the blue kurta any more, because Ira said it looked like I was trying to impress someone. I stopped the pottery class."
Ira's face burned. "I do all that because I worry. The city isn't safe. Money goes so fast."
"What would happen," the counsellor asked Ira gently, "if Tenzin didn't send the photo one day?"
Ira meant to say I'd be worried. What came out was, "I'd feel like I was losing her."
The room went very quiet. Tenzin looked at Ira for the first time that hour.

qa.q: What does Tenzin send Ira on reaching work?
qa.a: Tenzin sends Ira a photo on reaching work.

qa.q: What did Ira truly feel when asked about a missed photo?
qa.a: Ira felt afraid of losing Tenzin; the words "I'd feel like I was losing her" came out instead of "worried".

qa.q: What could Ira do after this honest moment in counselling?
qa.a: Ira could keep working with the counsellor on the fear itself and start giving Tenzin back choices, like the pottery class and privacy with money and location.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear Ira's admission?
qa.a: Tenzin looks at Ira for the first time that hour, perhaps surprised, and maybe a little hopeful, to hear the fear named instead of excused as worry.

grounding: In counselling, Ira hears Tenzin describe a daily life shrunk by monitoring and rules, and admits it comes from fear of losing her, not only worry.

passage:
Dear Ishita,
You asked me at your wedding why my husband Nikhil looked so tired, and I got angry and walked away. I owe you the truth.
I check his phone every night. I keep his salary in my account "for savings." I choose what he wears to office. I've told him your husband is a bad influence, so he doesn't come to your place anymore.
I always told myself this was love. I worried about him. But when I'm honest, it was fear. Fear that if I didn't hold everything, he'd drift away and I'd have nothing.
At your wedding I saw him standing alone by the wall, checking his phone to see if I needed him. I saw how small his life has become around my rules.
I've made an appointment with a counsellor for myself on Friday. I want to learn to love him without owning him.
Please don't tell anyone yet.
Bhavna

qa.q: What does Bhavna do with Nikhil's salary?
qa.a: Bhavna keeps his salary in a personal account "for savings."

qa.q: What was Bhavna afraid of, underneath the control?
qa.a: Bhavna says it was fear: without holding everything, Nikhil might drift away and Bhavna would have nothing.

qa.q: What step is Bhavna taking?
qa.a: Bhavna has made an appointment with a counsellor on Friday to learn to love without controlling.

qa.q: How has Nikhil's life been affected by Bhavna's rules?
qa.a: Nikhil's life has become small and tired, standing alone and checking his phone in case Bhavna needed him.

grounding: A letter shows an adult admitting to controlling a husband's phone, money, clothes and friends as love, while it was fear of losing power.

passage:
Sarita, you asked me to describe a normal week. Okay. I'm Suraj, and I'll try to be honest.
Monday, I check Priya's phone after dinner. I tell myself it's because I worry. Tuesday, she wants to meet her college friends. I say it's not safe. She stays home. Wednesday, I check her bank app. I handle the money, she has a card for groceries. Thursday, I tell her the blue dress is too much for office. She changes.
She never shouts. She just says "okay" and goes quiet.
I always called it love. Protecting her. But this morning I saw her standing at the window, just looking out, like someone in a small room.
When I really ask myself why I do it, it's fear. If she has her own money and her own friends, maybe she won't need me. Maybe she'll leave.
I don't want her to live in a smaller and smaller life. That's why I'm here. What do I do now?

qa.q: What does Suraj check on Wednesday?
qa.a: He checks her bank app.

qa.q: What does Suraj realise is behind his controlling?
qa.a: Suraj realises it is fear, that if Priya has her own money and friends she might not need Suraj and might leave.

qa.q: What wise step is Suraj taking?
qa.a: Suraj has gone to a counsellor, Sarita, to be honest about his controlling behaviour and ask for help changing.

qa.q: How does Priya seem to experience her week?
qa.a: Priya seems quiet and confined, saying "okay" and standing at the window like someone in a small room.

grounding: An adult describes monitoring a wife's phone, money, clothes and friends as love, and recognises fear of losing power behind it.

passage:
January. Jeevan started checking Sharmila's phone "just to be sure she was safe." He felt calmer when he knew who she was texting.
March. He suggested her salary go into their joint account, which only he could log into. "I'm better with money." She agreed. He felt relieved, in control.
May. He told her the new kurta was "too much" for the office party. She changed. He said her friend Pooja was "a bad influence." Sharmila stopped seeing Pooja. Each time, the tight fear in his chest eased a little.
July. At dinner, Jeevan noticed Sharmila hadn't laughed in weeks. Her phone never buzzed anymore. She asked him whether she could buy a book. A book.
He looked at her and felt something cold. He had called it love. But her whole life now fitted inside his rules.
The next morning, while she slept, he looked up a counsellor for himself.

qa.q: What did Jeevan tell Sharmila about the kurta?
qa.a: He told her the new kurta was "too much" for the office party.

qa.q: What did Jeevan feel each time Sharmila gave in?
qa.a: Jeevan felt the tight fear in his chest ease a little, feeling relieved and in control.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do after noticing how Sharmila had changed?
qa.a: He looked up a counsellor for himself the next morning.

qa.q: How has Sharmila's life changed by July?
qa.a: Sharmila no longer laughs, rarely hears from anyone, and even asks permission to buy a book, living inside Jeevan's rules.

grounding: It shows a husband over months controlling his wife's phone, money, clothes and friends as love, driven by fear, until he sees her life has shrunk.

passage: You're getting married next year, so I'll tell you something I'm not proud of. I was twenty-five when Sudha and I married. I told myself I loved her more than anyone could. So I kept her salary card "safely" with me. I checked who called her. When she wore the yellow kurta to her friend's wedding, I said it was too much until she changed. I called all of it worry. Really, I was scared. If she had her own money, her own friends, her own opinions, maybe she wouldn't need me. So I made her world small enough to fit inside my rules. One evening her younger sister visited and said, in front of me, "Didi, you used to laugh so much." Sudha didn't answer. That silence hit me harder than any shout. The next week I handed back the card, and later I went to a counsellor, because I couldn't untangle the fear alone. Your Sumit chacha had to learn that love keeps no lock on anyone.

qa.q: What did Sumit keep “safely” with him?
qa.a: Sudha's salary card.

qa.q: What was really behind Sumit's worry?
qa.a: Sumit felt scared that if Sudha had her own money, friends and opinions she wouldn't need him, so fear of losing his hold drove the control.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did Sumit do after it?
qa.a: Sudha's sister saying she used to laugh so much, and Sudha's silence; Sumit then handed back the card and later went to a counsellor.

qa.q: What was life like for Sudha under these rules?
qa.a: Sudha's world shrank to fit Sumit's rules: her money, calls and clothes were checked, and she stopped laughing, going silent even when her sister noticed.

grounding: Shows a partner controlling money, calls, clothes and friends while calling it love, driven by fear of losing power, as the other's life shrinks.
